claims.text: The initial alloy is a homogeneous, metastable single-phase solid solution produced by high-temperature melting and homogenization.
The unloaded single-phase baseline has high toughness and ductility.
Imposed mechanical stress drives local compositional fluctuations in the alloy.
Imposed mechanical stress drives short-range chemical ordering in the alloy.
Stress-driven compositional fluctuations or short-range ordering nucleate nanoscale embrittling features.
Stress-driven dislocation activity produces compositional fluctuations, nanoscale precipitates, or short-range ordered regions.
Applied stress enhances dislocation motion.
Enhanced dislocation motion locally disturbs the chemically uniform matrix.
Dislocation-induced disturbance of the matrix triggers short-range ordering or solute segregation.
Emergent ordered, segregated, or precipitated nanoscale features act as stress concentrators.
The emergent nanoscale features impede uniform plastic deformation.
Suppression of uniform plastic deformation lowers toughness and promotes brittle fracture.
Mechanically loaded samples will have lower fracture toughness than the unloaded baseline.
Mechanically loaded samples will initiate cracks earlier than the unloaded baseline.
Mechanically loaded samples will exhibit predominantly brittle fracture features.
TEM or atom-probe analysis of loaded samples will reveal compositional clustering or incipient nanoscale precipitates relative to the baseline.
The proposed embrittlement operates below conditions that cause complete phase transformation or recrystallization.
Very low strain rates or stresses insufficient to promote long-range dislocation activity may not trigger the proposed embrittlement.
The threshold stress and temperature for initiation of the proposed compositional changes are unknown.
Failure to detect loading-induced compositional changes or nanoscale precipitates, together with unchanged toughness and ductile fracture morphology, would reject the proposed mechanism.
